summary: Describes the ATM call control signaling exchanges needed to support Classical IP over ATM, as described in RFC 1577. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: How computers on an ATM network ask for and set up a connection so internet traffic can ride on it.

questions: what is atm signaling for ip
how does classical ip over atm set up a connection
what is the default ip mtu over atm aal5
subtitle: How an IP host or router should fill in ATM call setup messages so Classical IP over ATM interoperates.

tldr.problem: Classical IP over ATM (RFC 1577) and its encapsulation (RFC 1483) need ATM connections to be set up on demand, but ATM signaling offers many options and no single agreed way to use them for IP.
tldr.mechanism: This implementors guide says which signaling messages and information elements an IP-over-ATM endsystem must send in a SETUP, how to code them for AAL 5 and LLC/SNAP, how to manage and tear down multiple connections, and how to react when a call fails.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard written against ATM Forum UNI 3.1, with appendices for UNI 3.0 and Frame Relay interworking. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 1755 is a Proposed Standard from February 1995, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is tied to ATM Forum UNI 3.1, RFC 1577 and RFC 1483, and it says future revisions may use ATM capabilities that were not yet available.

sections.title: Why IP Needs ATM Signaling
sections.content:
In a Switched Virtual Connection (SVC) environment, ATM virtual channel connections are set up and released on demand. The ATM signaling protocol runs between an ATM endsystem and the ATM network. It sets up and releases calls (the association between ATM endpoints) and connections, uses addressing to find the other endpoint, allocates network resources, and lets the two ends agree on the end-to-end protocols they will use.

RFC 1755 is an implementors guide. It describes how IP over ATM implementations should use their local ATM signaling entity, following the ATM Forum User-Network Interface (UNI) Specification Version 3.1. It aims to help RFC 1577, RFC 1483 and UNI signaling interoperate, and it applies to IP hosts and routers that are also ATM endsystems.

IP address to ATM address resolution and routing are out of scope; they belong to the IP and ARP side defined in RFC 1577. Unless stated otherwise, the memo makes no distinction between the Private and Public UNI.
sections.eli5: ATM is like a phone network: you have to dial a call before you can talk. This memo explains how internet computers should dial and what to say.

sections.title: Opening, Sharing and Closing Connections
sections.content:
An endsystem may place an ATM call when it has a datagram to send and either no usable connection exists, it chooses not to use one (for route optimization or quality of service, for example), or the owner of the existing connection does not allow sharing. The owner of a connection is the entity within the endsystem that established it. If a connection uses LLC/SNAP encapsulation, the caller may send an InARP_REQUEST after receiving CONNECT and before its first data packet, and may send data without waiting for the InARP_REPLY.

Systems MUST be able to support multiple connections between the same pair of peers, whichever side opened each one. A receiver that accepts more than one call from one source MUST accept incoming PDUs on the extra connections, and SHOULD NOT accept a call only to close it or ignore its data. Because multiple connections are deliberately allowed, call collision avoidance algorithms such as the one in ISO/IEC 8473 MUST NOT be implemented. If configuration limits a destination to one connection, a colliding incoming call is rejected, and each side waits at least a configurable collision retry time of 1 to 10 seconds, plus a random increment with exponential backoff, before retrying.

Either endsystem may close a connection, and a datagram being sent at that moment is lost. Systems SHOULD allow a minimum holding time to be configured, with a suggested default of 60 seconds. Because public networks may charge for holding time, a system with a Public ATM UNI MUST support a configurable inactivity timer that watches traffic in both directions. A default of 20 minutes is RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: You may call a friend more than once at the same time, and your friend should not hang up on the extra calls. Do not hang up too fast, and hang up lines nobody is using so you are not charged for them.

sections.title: Call Setup and Release Messages
sections.content:
Point-to-point signaling uses a small set of messages. For setup these are SETUP, CALL PROCEEDING, CONNECT and CONNECT ACKNOWLEDGE. For release they are RELEASE and RELEASE COMPLETE.

The caller sends SETUP to the network. In its first response, either CALL PROCEEDING or CONNECT, the network gives the newly allocated VPCI/VCI. At the destination the network offers the call with its own SETUP. The destination answers with CONNECT (possibly preceded by CALL PROCEEDING), or with RELEASE COMPLETE if it cannot accept. Either endpoint, or rarely the network, can start a release: the party sends RELEASE, the other side answers RELEASE COMPLETE and resources are freed.

Each message holds mandatory and optional information elements (IEs), and the choice of IEs shapes the call. A SETUP for IP and multiprotocol interconnection MUST contain these IEs: AAL Parameters, ATM Traffic Descriptor, Broadband Bearer Capability, Broadband Low Layer Information, QoS Parameter, Called Party Number and Calling Party Number. UNI 3.1 makes the AAL Parameters and Broadband Low Layer Information IEs optional, but for IP over ATM they MUST be included. Appendix A of the RFC shows a sample coded SETUP and CONNECT.
sections.eli5: A call starts with a SETUP, like dialing. The other side answers CONNECT, like picking up, or says it cannot take the call. Hanging up is also a two-step exchange so both sides know it is over.

sections.title: Adaptation Layer and Encapsulation Settings
sections.content:
Two IEs are meaningful mainly to the two endpoints. The AAL Parameters IE says which ATM Adaptation Layer to use. Because RFC 1483 specifies IP over AAL 5, AAL 5 MUST be indicated in the AAL type field. The forward and backward maximum CPCS-SDU size fields can range from zero to 65,535. The default IP MTU over AAL 5 is 9188 bytes, but endstations are encouraged to support MTU sizes up to and including 64k. No service specific convergence sublayer is normally used, so the SSCS type SHOULD be absent or coded as Null SSCS.

The Broadband Low Layer Information (B-LLI) IE selects the encapsulation. RFC 1577 makes LLC/SNAP the default, and every endstation MUST implement it. LLC is signaled with layer 2 id 2 and user information layer 12 (lan_llc, ISO 8802/2). A B-LLI that names both LLC and a SNAP layer 3 id is not recommended, because it is left to the LLC layer to read the SNAP header and hand IP packets upward.

A caller MAY use an extended B-LLI (layer 3 id 3, ISO/IEC TR 9577 IPI 204, which is 0xCC) to say that IP manages the call and the circuit carries only IP. Called parties MUST accept this, and the caller MUST still use LLC/SNAP encapsulation on every datagram, because the receiver may choose to ignore the layer 3 information. Signaling for null-encapsulated circuits is only mentioned, and processing it is not required.

A caller that supports more than one encapsulation can send up to three B-LLI instances in descending order of preference. The called side picks the first one it supports and returns it in CONNECT. If it supports none, it clears the call with cause #88, incompatible destination. If the SETUP has no B-LLI at all, the call is cleared with cause #21, call rejected.
sections.eli5: Both sides must agree on how big a package can be and how it is wrapped. The wrapping everybody must know is the default one, and a caller can list a few favorites in order, like asking for a blue box first, then a red one.

sections.title: Traffic, Bearer, QoS and Address Elements
sections.content:
Other IEs matter to the network as well as the endpoints. The ATM Traffic Descriptor describes the connection by peak cell rate, sustainable cell rate and maximum burst size. IP behaves most naturally like the Best Effort Capability, which carries no guarantees and may deliver zero throughput at any time. When the network offers it, it MAY be requested with the Best Effort indicator plus peak cell rates for both directions. Every IP over ATM endsystem MUST support three parameter combinations in SETUP: a token-bucket style description, a constant bit rate description meant for ATM pipes such as router to router, and Best Effort. Without Best Effort, link rate SHOULD NOT be requested as the peak cell rate, and a fraction such as 1/10th of the link bandwidth is RECOMMENDED.

The Broadband Bearer Capability IE must allow both BCOB-C and BCOB-X in the combinations the memo lists. The QoS Parameter IE uses the Unspecified class (Class 0), the only class all networks must support and the only one allowed with Best Effort. Classes 3 and 4 may apply but must be arranged with the network provider. UNI offers no negotiation of traffic, bearer or QoS values, so the caller SHOULD already know what the network and the called party will accept.

For addressing, the Called Party Number and Calling Party Number IEs carry the ATM addresses. RFC 1577 recommends that a router be able to serve several logical IP subnets on one physical interface. The Selector (SEL) field can separate up to 256 of them for one ESI, and it is the only recommended use of SEL. Native E.164 addresses have no SEL field, so multiple E.164 addresses are RECOMMENDED there.
sections.eli5: The call also says how much speed you want and how careful the network must be. Internet traffic is happy with whatever is left over, so the usual request is simply the do-your-best kind.

sections.title: When a Call Fails
sections.content:
Some causes in a RELEASE or RELEASE COMPLETE mean the destination cannot be reached, and SHOULD be treated as Network Unreachable (for a router) or Host Unreachable (for a host), as in RFC 1122. These are #1 unallocated number, #3 no route to destination, #17 user busy, #18 no user responding, #27 destination out of order, #38 network out of order, #41 temporary failure and #47 resource unavailable.

Other causes mean the request might work if changed, so the endsystem MAY retry with different IEs. Examples are #37 user cell rate unavailable (try smaller rates), #73 unsupported combination of traffic parameter (try another combination), #57 and #58 for the bearer capability, #49 quality of service unavailable (try another class), #88 incompatible destination and #78 AAL parameter cannot be supported. The called side, for its part, SHOULD clear the call with #37 if it cannot handle cells at the forward peak cell rate indicated.
sections.eli5: If nobody answers or the line is dead, the computer treats the other side as unreachable. If the other side just did not like your request, you can phone again and ask in a different way.

sections.title: UNI 3.0 and Frame Relay Appendices
sections.content:
UNI 3.1 is described as an erratum to UNI 3.0, produced largely to align with Recommendation Q.2931, but the two versions are incompatible in several ways. Appendix B explains IP over ATM with UNI 3.0. The Traffic Descriptor is called the ATM User Cell Rate IE, the AAL maximum SDU size runs from one (not zero) to 64K, and the cause numbers differ: user cell rate unavailable is #51 (not #37) and AAL parameter cannot be supported is #93 (not #78). The AAL 'mode' field SHOULD be omitted and MUST be ignored by the destination.

Appendix D covers interworking with Frame Relay. An endsystem that wants the Frame Relay SSCS (FR-SSCS) must signal both FR-SSCS and RFC 1490 encapsulation in SETUP. Neither LLC encapsulation nor VC-multiplexing interoperates over FR-SSCS, so they cannot be offered as alternatives to it. This makes it hard for an ATM host calling a host behind an interworking unit, because it will ask for LLC, and the unit may accept and translate, or reject and call back using FR-SSCS.
sections.eli5: An older version of the phone rules used slightly different names and numbers, so the memo lists the differences. Talking to a different kind of network needs extra steps, because the two wrap their packages differently.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC is short on this point. It says that not all security issues of IP over ATM are clearly understood, because of the fluid state of ATM specifications and the newness of the technology. Future revisions were expected to address whatever security capabilities later signaling standards might offer. The memo defines no security mechanism itself.
sections.eli5: The authors admit they do not yet know all the ways this could be attacked, and they promise to add safety rules later.
